answers.answer: Caching could avoid repeating the 80 ms guide-building database work for the frequently reused station-language pairs, using a 2 ms cache lookup on hits. Weekly changes make reuse plausible, provided the team chooses an acceptable staleness/update policy. A key such as station-guide:123:es includes both station ID and requested language, so English and Spanish do not share the wrong result. On a hit, the API returns the cached guide without this database lookup. On a miss, the API reads/builds the guide from the database, stores the result in the cache, and returns it. The application does both the database read and cache fill; the cache does not fetch independently. The database remains authoritative.

evidence.quote: Keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page.
Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.
The API finds product:42 in the cache and returns its stored details.
The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. A already fetched them before B committed. Deletion at step 3 did not cancel that fetched value or prevent A from storing it afterward at step 4. C therefore hits the stale value before expiry. The team cannot claim that every read after B finishes sees new hours: C is the counterexample. A simple way to avoid serving this stale copy for a latest-committed-hours endpoint is to bypass this cache and have the API read the authoritative database for each request. Under the question's exact sequence and the declared commit prerequisite, C's database read would see the new hours. The lesson does not teach a general concurrency protocol, and none is needed for that bypass.

evidence.quote: These steps are not atomic. Removal can fail, or an overlapping read can put an older value back after removal.
A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. For checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.

answers.answer: In case A, the 12:03 request can use the original cached forecast, although it became stale when the source changed at 12:02. The original entry expires at 12:10; the 12:11 request must fetch the source because expired entries cannot be served and there is no background refresh. In case B, removal at 12:04 leaves no original entry, so the 12:05 request must fetch the source despite being before 12:10. The ten-minute TTL sets the original entry's maximum permitted lifetime before expiry; it does not promise ten minutes of source freshness, refresh when the source changes, or automatically reload at 12:10. It also does not guarantee the entry remains present for the full ten minutes. Memory removal is eviction to make room, rather than expiration due to elapsed TTL.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: Today, deleting the writer instance's local copy leaves the other three instances' copies unchanged. Requests routed to those instances can hit the old map, while the writer instance must reload on its next miss. A single shared cache entry is the simpler fit for the stated goal: all four instances look up that entry, so one deletion removes the cached map for every instance; with no concurrent fills, a subsequent miss reloads the updated database map. Independent local caches avoid network lookups but require separate handling to remove every copy. The shared cache adds the accepted 2 ms network lookup and a separate service to operate. If that service fails, fallback requests can overload the database unless fallback work is limited. Sharing itself does not make database updates automatically invalidate the entry.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.
Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.
A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.

answers.answer: When the popular key expires, many simultaneous misses could each issue the same database read, exceeding the safe 500 reads per second. Coalesce these requests: let one request initiate the schedule database lookup and have concurrent readers share that in-progress lookup and its result, instead of each starting another database read. The application can fill the cache with that result. During the separate full-cache outage, blindly falling back could turn almost all 10,000 requests per second into database reads, far above capacity. Limit admitted fallback database reads to at most the safe 500 per second and return temporary errors to excess requests. This reduces actual database work by refusing excess reads rather than merely delaying the same immediate flood. If a last-known schedule is accessible despite the cache outage, it can be returned within the permitted 60-second window to avoid more reads; do not serve it beyond that permission, and use errors when no permissible copy is available. The lesson does not specify where such an outage-accessible old copy is stored, so the bounded fallback plus error response does not depend on one.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.
A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
Falling back to the database is a load decision, not a free recovery path.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Every uniquely identified result is read exactly once, so filling after that database read produces no later reader to reuse it and saves no database reads. The current 2 ms database read fits comfortably within the 100 ms budget, and ten reads per second is below the stated 1,000-read capacity. The proposal adds a copy to store and manage and a cache fill for each result without the intended reuse benefit. Reconsider if results begin receiving repeated reads, especially if a small set accounts for many requests, or those repeated database reads become a latency or capacity problem. Measure response time, database load, hits, and misses to establish whether caching then helps.

evidence.quote: First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track the fraction of lookups that hit, and what happens during misses.
